``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} Draft: figures transcribed from RSPB Research Report 76 are still being checked against the original tables. ::: ## The short version - At the nine Scottish SPAs surveyed for **Great Skua**, breeding territories fell from 6,570 to 1,524 (**-77%**). - At six Scottish **Northern Gannet** SPAs, nest counts fell from 169,054 to 131,361 (**-22%**). Against a baseline projected forward for pre-outbreak growth, the fall is **-28%**. - Not every species declined everywhere. Guillemot counts, for example, rose at some SPAs and fell at others. - These are before-and-after counts at surveyed sites. They show a large drop that coincides with the outbreak, but on their own they cannot prove how much of it HPAI caused. ## What this measures The change in the number of breeding seabirds at Scottish Special Protection Areas (SPAs) between a **pre-outbreak baseline** (mostly from the Seabirds Count census, 2015 to 2021) and a **coordinated survey in 2023**, after highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI H5N1) caused mass seabird deaths in 2021 and 2022. Counts are of breeding units: apparently occupied nests, sites, or territories, or individual birds for Guillemot. ## Why it matters Scotland holds internationally important seabird populations, many protected by SPAs under the Habitats Regulations. HPAI arrived on top of existing declines: the Seabirds Count census found that most seabird species in Scotland had already declined since the previous census. Seabird abundance and breeding success are OSPAR and UK Marine Strategy indicators of marine bird status. ## Reading this like an outbreak investigation ::: {.grid} ::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6} **What the data can tell us** - **Magnitude:** how much smaller breeding numbers were in 2023 at the sites surveyed. - **Distribution:** which species and which colonies changed most. - **Timing:** the drop coincides with the outbreak, and for some species it is far outside their recent trend. ::: ::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6} **What it cannot tell us on its own** - **Cause:** there is no unexposed comparison group, so this is a before-after design. Other pressures were operating at the same time. - **Mechanism:** fewer breeding birds could mean deaths, or survivors skipping a breeding season. - **The full picture:** only surveyed sites are included, and mortality after early 2023 is not captured. ::: ::: The epidemiological questions behind each chart: 1. **Is the change real or noise?** The forest plot shows each colony's change with a confidence interval. 2. **What would have happened anyway?** For Gannet, the report projects each colony's pre-outbreak trend forward to 2021. Comparing against that projection is like adjusting for a secular trend. 3. **Who was counted?** Coverage (the share of the population surveyed) works like a response rate, and it varies a lot between species. ## Trend and status ### UK picture: 13 species ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](seabirds_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='Dot chart of percentage change in UK breeding counts between the pre-outbreak baseline and 2023 for 13 seabird species. Point size shows the percentage of the UK population counted. Great Skua shows the largest decline at minus 76 percent.' width=1350} ::: ::: ### Colony by colony: Great Skua and Gannet ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](seabirds_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-alt='Forest plot of percentage change in breeding counts at Scottish Special Protection Areas for Great Skua and Northern Gannet, with 95 percent confidence intervals. All Great Skua colonies fell by 40 to 86 percent. Gannet colonies fell by 3 to 37 percent.' width=1500} ::: ::: The confidence intervals are narrow because these are large counts. That makes them a **minimum** estimate of uncertainty: they reflect counting noise only, not observer error, survey timing, or differences between baseline years. Even so, the Great Skua declines are far too large and too consistent to be explained by noise. ### Gannet: how much depends on the baseline? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](seabirds_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-alt='Dumbbell chart for six Gannet SPAs comparing percentage change from the observed baseline with percentage change from a trend-adjusted 2021 baseline. The adjusted decline is larger at colonies whose baseline was counted several years before the outbreak.' width=1500} ::: ::: Gannet colonies were growing before the outbreak, and some baselines date from 2014. Comparing 2023 with the counted baseline gives **-22%**. Comparing it with each colony's projected 2021 size gives **-28%**. This is the same logic as adjusting for a secular trend: if a population was rising, a simple before-after comparison understates the impact. ## Map ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## All Scottish SPA results ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Notes on starred rows (from the report):** - Forth Islands (Northern Gannet): 2023 figure is a preliminary estimate (approx. 55,000). - North Rona and Sula Sgeir (Northern Gannet): Low confidence in 2023 count (high observer variation). - Ailsa Craig (Northern Gannet): Low confidence in 2023 count (high observer variation). 95% CI reflects counting noise only. % counted: share of the SPA population surveyed in 2023 (blank where not reported). Units: AON/AOS/AOT = apparently occupied nests/sites/territories; IND = individual birds. Species with small colonies (for example Arctic Skua, with single-figure counts at some SPAs) are included for completeness but say little on their own. ## Confidence **Medium.** The 2023 survey was large and coordinated, and for Great Skua, Gannet, and the terns it covered most of the population. But: - Baseline years vary (2014 to 2021), so some of each change happened before the outbreak. - A few 2023 counts are flagged by the report authors as preliminary or low confidence. - Coverage is low for some species, so totals may not represent the whole population. ## Limitations - **Attribution:** the report's authors consider HPAI the main driver for Great Skua, Gannet, and Roseate Tern, and likely for Sandwich and Common Tern. For species already in long-term decline, separating HPAI from other pressures is harder. This page reports change; it does not estimate a causal effect. - **Breeding numbers only:** the data do not include breeding success or adult survival. - **Incomplete timing:** further HPAI deaths in 2023 happened after these counts. - **Transcription:** SPA figures were transcribed from the report's PDF tables (table and page recorded for each row) and checked against printed totals where available. ## Optional next step With approved access to the Seabird Monitoring Programme database (BTO/JNCC), annual counts at monitored colonies would show whether populations have started to recover since 2023, and allow a proper interrupted time-series analysis. Any such analysis would follow the SMP data use policy. ## Data sources and licences - Tremlett, C.J., Morley, N. and Wilson, L.J.
